views.rationale:
RECOMMENDATION: Keep the May 10 List 3 hike and the May 15 Huawei/ICT measures in place, leave the proposed remaining Chinese-import list as a comment-period threat rather than an immediate duty, and reopen talks on the April draft—especially written legal changes and an enforcement mechanism. Do not roll back tariffs or trade structural demands for purchase pledges. Use the June 1 Chinese effective date and any Trump–Xi/G20 window to test whether Beijing will restore the commitments it walked back.

SUPPORTING RATIONALE: Threat is a modest US opportunity, not an existential hit. After months of reported progress (Apr 3 talks on enforcement text; Feb 24 delay of the List 3 hike), US officials said China retreated from commitments to write IP/tech-transfer and related reforms into law; Trump on May 5 ordered List 3 from 10 percent to 25 percent (effective May 10) and preparation of tariffs on remaining Chinese imports. That restored leverage: the US already covers about 250 billion dollars at 25 percent, China’s announced reply is a rate hike on an existing 60 billion dollar US list (many lines June 1), and the bilateral imbalance still limits Beijing’s tariff ammunition. US consumer sentiment printed 100 in May and CPI is contained; Chinese industrial production cooled to about 5 percent year over year. The opportunity is incomplete: US goods exports to China remain weak, Midwest agriculture is the exposed sector, 10-year yields fell to 2.37 percent and VIX jumped to 20.55 on May 13, and contemporaneous Oxford/Goldman readings already put tariff incidence on US firms and households. Immediate implementation of the remaining-import list would land on apparel, footwear, and consumer electronics and invite a deeper spiral; a rollback now would reward the walk-back. Negotiation without new US concessions is therefore the stance that matches both the leverage and the self-harm risk.
key_factors: China walk-back from April draft legal/enforcement commitments
List 3 already raised to 25 percent on about 200 billion dollars (May 10); remaining-import list proposed but not implemented
Huawei entity-list / EO 13873 opened a separate tech-security track (May 15)
Asymmetric trade: US can still tax remaining Chinese goods; China is mostly repricing an existing 60 billion dollar list effective June 1
US macro still resilient (UMCSENT 100) vs farm-belt and market stress (yields, VIX, ag aid)
Talks not dead: Liu He still came to Washington; both sides left a June 1 / possible leader-level off-ramp

sources_cited.excerpt: Trump tweets negotiations going too slowly and China attempting to renegotiate; orders List 3 raised from 10% to 25% on May 10 and preparation of tariffs on remaining ~$300B.
List 3 tariff rate rises from 10% to 25%.
China announces it will raise retaliatory tariff rates on its ~$60B US-goods list (higher rates phased in; many effective June 1).
Trump signs Executive Order 13873 (securing ICT supply chains). Commerce moves to restrict Huawei.
Intensive Washington talks; both sides report progress on text, including enforcement language. No final deal signed.
University of Michigan consumer sentiment latest 100 (2019-05-01), still elevated.
10-year Treasury yield 2.37% on 2019-05-15, down 0.69pp over the window; sold off to 2.40% on May 13 after China’s retaliation announcement.
VIX spiked to 20.55 on 2019-05-13 then eased to 16.44 on 2019-05-15.
US goods imports from China down ~14.8% over the window (latest $39.0B).
China industrial production index 105.0 in May 2019 (about 5% y/y), softer than March’s 108.5.

No progress as Liu defended changes via State Council decrees; Lighthizer insisted on restoration of previous text. Trump in absolutely no rush. Oxford Economics: higher tariffs could cut US GDP 0.3% and China 0.8% in 2020.
May 13 proposal: 25% on remaining ~$300B (essentially all uncovered products, including apparel/footwear/food); excludes pharma, rare earths, critical minerals.
Farm Bureau: China’s June 1 hike hits US farmers at every single angle; Trump floated about 15 billion dollars in farm aid.
Commerce adding Huawei and 70 affiliates to the Entity List, restricting US-origin parts without a license.
Mnuchin: weekend communications showed talks going substantially backwards, including China backing off writing some economic-practice changes into law.
